text: This is an illustrative scenario, not a real reported incident. Harrow Creek Goods ships a nightly reporting CronJob, copied from an older manifest and trimmed down -- without anyone noticing the trim also removed the entire resources block, leaving the container with no CPU or memory ceiling at all.

On most nights the export finishes quickly using little memory. One night, an upstream schema change makes the query return a much larger result set, and the report container's memory use climbs steadily instead of finishing. With no memory limit set, nothing inside Kubernetes tells the kernel to stop that growth.

kubectl get pods afterward shows three failures on the same node: the report container itself errored out, order-worker shows OOMKilled, and order-api shows Evicted. Neither order-worker nor order-api had anything wrong with their own manifests -- both were healthy, correctly configured pods caught in a neighbor's blast radius.

OOMKilled and Evicted are two different mechanisms responding to the same memory pressure. OOMKilled means the Linux kernel's own OOMKiller picked a specific process and killed it once memory truly ran out. Evicted means the kubelet itself proactively removed a pod from the node to relieve system-wide pressure, before the kernel had to step in at all.

The direct fix adds requests and limits to the report container -- a 512Mi memory limit means the same runaway query gets that one container OOMKilled on its own, a contained and expected failure, instead of destabilizing its neighbors. The platform-wide fix is a LimitRange on every namespace, which supplies safe default requests and limits automatically to any future container that forgets its own.

This incident is a reminder that a pod's own correct configuration doesn't protect it from an unlimited neighbor sharing its node. Lesson 32 closes the chapter by tracing every decision across this capstone's three lessons -- and the rest of the course -- back to the chapter that made each one possible.
